stem: A company moves a payroll server to a cloud provider. The provider patches the hypervisor. The company's administrators still patch the guest operating system and the payroll application. Which service model is this, and who owns the guest OS?
choices: Infrastructure as a service, and the company owns the guest operating system
Software as a service, and the company patches the provider's mail platform
Platform as a service, and the company patches the underlying operating system
A cold site, because the server is not in the basement
explanation: In IaaS you rent infrastructure and you still operate the guest. SaaS is a finished application you do not patch. PaaS gives you a runtime and the provider owns the OS underneath your code. Being off-premises does not make a workload a cold site. A cold site is an empty recovery location.
choiceNotes: The company patches the guest. That is IaaS. The provider owns the hardware and the hypervisor.
SaaS would mean the provider runs the application and the company does not patch a server OS.
PaaS customers do not patch the platform operating system. They bring the application.
A cold site has no running payroll server. This server is in production.

stem: Under a typical shared-responsibility model, which duty stays with the customer in every model, including software as a service?
choices: Deciding who may access the customer's data and how that data is classified
Patching the provider's hypervisor
Replacing the provider's physical disks
Writing the provider's hypervisor code
explanation: The customer keeps ownership of the data and of the identities that may see it, even when the provider runs the application. The hypervisor, the disks, and the provider's source code are the provider's problem in SaaS. People mix this up by assuming 'the cloud' absorbed the access reviews. It did not.
choiceNotes: Data and access decisions stay with the customer. A SaaS mail admin still has to remove a terminated employee.
The hypervisor is below the customer's view in SaaS and in most IaaS contracts. The customer does not patch it.
Physical disks in the provider's region are not the customer's to swap.
The customer does not maintain the provider's product source.

stem: An application is split into small services that talk over APIs. Each service can be deployed without rebuilding the others. A networking design moves decisions about where traffic may flow into a central controller, while the devices just forward. Which two architecture ideas are those? (Choose two.)
choices: Microservices
Software-defined networking
A single monolithic binary with no internal APIs
A hub that floods every port
explanation: Microservices are independently deployable pieces behind APIs. Software-defined networking separates the control plane, where policy lives, from the data plane, which forwards. A monolith is the opposite of microservices. A hub is a dumb repeater, not a controller-driven fabric.
choiceNotes: Independent services behind APIs are microservices. You can ship one without rebuilding the rest.
A central controller with simple forwarders is software-defined networking.
A monolith is one deployable unit. It is the architecture microservices leave behind.
A hub floods frames. It has no separate control plane for security policy.

stem: Developers describe servers in files, review the files, and a pipeline creates matching infrastructure. Last night someone changed a firewall by hand and the next pipeline run reverted it. What practice is the pipeline enforcing?
choices: Infrastructure as code, which treats the reviewed file as the source of truth
Shadow IT, which is the approved process
A honeyfile
Steganography
explanation: Infrastructure as code makes the reviewed definition win over a one-off click. The revert felt rude and it prevented drift. The hand change needs to be proposed in the file if it was actually required. Shadow IT is unsanctioned tech. A honeyfile and steganography are not deployment pipelines.
choiceNotes: The file is the source of truth. A hand change that is not in the file is drift, and the pipeline removed it.
Shadow IT avoids the approved process. This pipeline is the approved process.
A honeyfile is a decoy document. It does not build firewalls.
Steganography hides data inside other data. It does not declare infrastructure.

stem: A container image runs many copies of one service on a cluster. A virtual machine next to it runs a full guest operating system for a legacy app. Which statement is accurate?
choices: The container shares the host kernel and is lighter. The virtual machine includes its own guest kernel and isolates the legacy OS
Containers include a unique guest kernel every time, so they are always heavier than virtual machines
A virtual machine cannot run an old operating system
Containers and virtual machines are the same isolation boundary
explanation: Containers package an application and use the host kernel, which is why they start fast and why a kernel bug can matter to every container. A VM virtualizes hardware and boots a guest kernel, which is the right place for an OS you cannot put on the host. They are not the same boundary. Legacy operating systems are a standard reason to keep a VM.
choiceNotes: Shared kernel versus a guest kernel is the practical difference. Pick the VM when the legacy OS cannot share the host kernel.
Containers are lighter because they do not boot a private kernel. The weight comparison is backwards.
A VM is often how you keep an old OS. The statement that it cannot is false.
The isolation models differ. Treating them as identical leads to the wrong patch and the wrong threat model.

stem: A function runs in response to uploads. The team does not patch an operating system for it and they do not choose the host. They do control the function's identity and the bucket policy. What is this model?
choices: Serverless
A colocation cage where the team owns the racks
An on-premises mainframe they administer
A cold spare server in the closet
explanation: Serverless, or functions as a service, hides the server. You still own the code, the permissions, and the data policy. Those are the usual places serverless breaches actually happen. Colocation and a mainframe put the operating system back on your list. A cold spare is powered off hardware.
choiceNotes: No host to patch, but the identity and the data policy remain yours. That is serverless.
A cage means you still rack and often still patch machines. That is not this function.
A mainframe you administer is the opposite of 'we do not choose the host.'
A cold spare is unused hardware. It does not run on each upload.

stem: An industrial controller runs a real-time operating system and cannot be patched on the office monthly cycle without stopping a production line. It is reachable from the corporate network. What architecture change is the security priority?
choices: Segment the controller onto a network the office cannot browse, and tightly limit any path that must exist
Join the controller to the same flat network as guest Wi-Fi for easier vendor access
Expose its management port to the internet so the vendor can patch ad hoc
Replace segmentation with a longer password on the guest Wi-Fi
explanation: Operational technology should not sit on the IT LAN. A real-time controller that you cannot patch casually needs a boundary more than it needs convenience. Vendor access, if required, is a controlled path, not an internet-facing management port and not the guest network. A Wi-Fi password does not segment a plant.
choiceNotes: Put the controller on its own segment and allow only named, necessary flows. That is the architecture fix.
Guest Wi-Fi is an untrusted network. Merging it with a controller increases exposure.
An internet-facing management port is a permanent attack surface on a device you cannot patch quickly.
A guest password does not create a boundary between IT and the plant.

stem: Administrators currently SSH from the internet to every server. The new design allows SSH only from one hardened host, and that host is the only one that may reach the servers. What is the hardened host?
choices: A jump server
A honeypot
A cold site
A CRL
explanation: A jump server, or jump host, is the bastion administrators pass through. The servers no longer accept management traffic from the whole internet, so you can harden and log one door. A honeypot is a decoy. A cold site is a recovery room. A CRL is a list of revoked certificates.
choiceNotes: The jump server is the single management path. Restrict SSH to it and watch it closely.
A honeypot should not be the path real administrators use to reach production.
A cold site is empty space for recovery. It is not an SSH gateway.
A CRL lists revoked certificates. It does not proxy administrator sessions.

stem: A device sits inline and can drop a connection that matches a signature. A second device receives a copy of traffic from a mirror and can only alert. Which is which?
choices: The inline device is an IPS. The mirror-fed device is an IDS
Both are routers
The alerting device is the IPS because it is more careful
The inline device is a jump server
explanation: Prevention requires being in the path so the device can drop the packet. Detection can work from a copy. An IPS is inline. An IDS often is not, and therefore cannot stop the original packet. Carefulness does not rename the architecture. A jump server is an admin bastion, not an inspection engine.
choiceNotes: Inline and able to drop is prevention. Copy and alert is detection.
Routers forward. They are not defined by signature drops versus alerts.
Alert-only is detection. Being careful does not put the device in the forwarding path.
A jump server is where administrators log in. It does not inspect a mirror.

stem: A public website must be reachable from the internet and must not sit on the same subnet as payroll. The design places it between an outer and an inner firewall. What is that zone?
choices: A screened subnet
The native VLAN of the user access layer
A honeynet full of production payroll data
A cold site
explanation: A screened subnet, still often called a DMZ, is where systems the internet must reach live, separated from the internal network. If the web server is compromised, the inner firewall is still in the way. Putting it on the user VLAN removes that wall. A honeynet should not hold payroll. A cold site is not the live web tier.
choiceNotes: The screened subnet is the in-between zone for the public site. Payroll stays behind the inner firewall.
The user VLAN is an internal network. A public site does not belong there with payroll.
A honeynet is a decoy network. Production payroll does not go in it.
A cold site is a recovery location, not the place you serve the website today.

stem: A security appliance loses power and stops processing. Traffic that used to flow through it now passes with no inspection. Which failure mode is that, and why do security teams usually avoid it for a firewall?
choices: Fail-open. A firewall that fails open stops enforcing policy, so the usual security choice is fail-closed
Fail-closed, because traffic continuing means the policy is still applied
Fail-open is always required by fire code for every firewall
Failure mode is only a disk RAID term
explanation: Fail-open means the path stays up and the control stops. Fail-closed means the path stops when the control stops, so uninspected traffic does not flow. For a firewall, fail-closed is the secure default. Fail-open can be a conscious availability choice, and it is a different discussion for a life-safety door that must let people out. It is not 'always required' for firewalls, and it is not a RAID term.
choiceNotes: Traffic continuing without inspection is fail-open. Security firewalls are usually set to fail closed so a dead box does not become a wire.
If traffic continues with no policy, the control is not closed. The label is backwards.
Fire code can require doors to fail open so people can exit. That does not set every firewall to pass all packets.
RAID is disk redundancy. Fail-open and fail-closed describe what a control does when it breaks.

stem: Remote workers must reach file servers, and policy says their web browsing also has to pass through company filtering. A VPN that sends only the file-server subnets through the tunnel leaves browsing on the home internet. What is wrong with that design for this policy?
choices: It is split tunneling, so browsing never sees the company filter
It is a full tunnel, so browsing is already filtered
Split tunneling encrypts the home browsing with the company proxy automatically
The design is a screened subnet
explanation: Split tunneling sends selected networks through the VPN and lets the rest go direct. Direct browsing skips the corporate filter. A full tunnel would send all traffic in, which is what this policy requires, at a cost in bandwidth and user experience. The traffic that never enters the tunnel is not inspected by the company. A screened subnet is a zone on a firewall, not a laptop routing mode.
choiceNotes: Split tunnel is the exemption. This policy wants the browsing inside the tunnel.
A full tunnel would include the browsing. The proposal does not.
Traffic that leaves via the home router is not magically proxied at the company.
A screened subnet is where a public server sits. It is not this VPN mode.

stem: A web application firewall, a TLS-inspecting proxy, and a network firewall that only understands IP addresses and ports are proposed for the same public app. Which job belongs to the web application firewall?
choices: Inspecting HTTP requests for application attacks such as injection patterns
Replacing the need for any network firewall
Encrypting the disk of the database server
Issuing badges for the lobby
explanation: A WAF understands the web protocol and can block classes of application abuse that a pure address-and-port firewall cannot see. It does not replace network policy, encrypt disks, or run the lobby. TLS inspection is how a proxy or a firewall can see inside encrypted web traffic. It is related and it is not the same product as the WAF's rule set.
choiceNotes: The WAF is the application-layer inspection. Port 443 being 'allowed' is not enough.
You still want a network firewall. The WAF is an additional control, not a substitute for every other one.
Disk encryption is a data-at-rest control on the server. It is not request inspection.
Badges are physical identity. A WAF does not print them.

stem: Wireless users must authenticate with individual directory accounts before the access point grants network access. A shared passphrase is not acceptable. Which pair of technologies fits?
choices: 802.1X with RADIUS
WEP with a posted key
A hidden SSID and no authentication
A hub and a longer Ethernet cable
explanation: 802.1X is the port-based authentication framework. RADIUS is the usual server that checks the directory account. The access point is the authenticator and the laptop is the supplicant. WEP and an open hidden network do not give per-user accounts. A hub does not authenticate anyone.
choiceNotes: 802.1X plus RADIUS is how each person uses a directory account on Wi-Fi.
WEP is a broken shared key. It cannot disable one person without changing everyone's key.
Hiding the name is not authentication. An open network accepts anyone who finds it.
A hub repeats frames. It does not check directory accounts.

stem: An architect places user laptops, the public website, and the database in one subnet 'to keep routing simple,' and relies on host firewalls that administrators often disable. What principle is being ignored?
choices: Defense in depth and shrinking the blast radius. One flat subnet means a single host firewall is the only barrier
The principle that one control is always enough if it is expensive
The idea that databases should be reachable from the internet by default
Simplicity is always the enemy, so routing should be made confusing on purpose
explanation: Defense in depth stacks independent controls so one mistake is not the whole breach. A flat subnet plus a host firewall people can turn off is one control. The website and the database should not share a trust zone with laptops. You do not add confusion for its own sake. You add boundaries that match the data.
choiceNotes: Separate the zones and do not let a disableable host firewall be the only control between laptops and the database.
Price does not make a single control sufficient. The architect removed the other layers.
Databases should not be generally reachable from the internet or from user laptops.
The goal is clear boundaries, not mystery. Simple routing can still have separate subnets.

stem: A database page is being read and modified in memory by the database process. A backup tape of last night sits in a safe. Users download a report over TLS. Which state is the in-memory page?
choices: Data in use
Data at rest
Data in transit
Data that no longer needs access control
explanation: Data in use is being processed. Data at rest is stored, such as the tape. Data in transit is crossing a network, such as the TLS download. In-use data is the awkward state because it has to be readable by the process. Access control still applies. Memory scraping is why people care about this state.
choiceNotes: The page in memory is in use. Encryption and access control still matter, and they are harder here than on the tape.
The tape in the safe is the at-rest copy. The memory page is not sitting in storage.
TLS covers the download, which is transit. The memory page has not been sent yet.
Being in memory does not cancel access control. The process identity still matters.

stem: A payment form shows only the last four digits of a card number to a support agent. The real number is replaced in the application database by a value that means nothing without a separate vault. Which two techniques are those? (Choose two.)
choices: Masking
Tokenization
Hashing the card number and throwing away the vault so charges can still be made
Printing the full number on the receipt for convenience
explanation: Masking limits what a person sees. Tokenization swaps the sensitive value for a token, and the real value stays in a controlled vault so the business can still transact. A hash you cannot reverse, with no vault, cannot be charged later. Printing the full number undoes both controls.
choiceNotes: Showing only the last four digits is masking. The agent does not need the rest.
A token that requires a vault is tokenization. The database does not hold the raw card number.
A one-way hash without a vault cannot be turned back into a chargeable card number. That breaks the business process this design kept.
Printing the full number is disclosure. It is the failure both techniques exist to prevent.

stem: Customer records must stay in a specific country because of a privacy law. An architect proposes a replica in another region because it is cheaper. The law does not allow that replica. What requirement is the architect about to break?
choices: Data sovereignty
A preference for a particular font
The 100-meter copper limit
A screensaver timeout
explanation: Data sovereignty means the data is subject to the laws of the place it sits, and some data is not allowed to leave. Cheaper storage in another region is not a reason to move it. Fonts, copper length, and screensavers are unrelated. The control is region selection, contractual limits, and technical blocks on replication.
choiceNotes: The law follows the data to the region. A forbidden replica is a sovereignty breach even if the disks are fine.
A font is presentation. It does not decide where records may live.
Copper length limits a LAN link. It does not choose a legal region.
A screensaver locks a screen. It does not govern cross-border copies.

stem: A data loss prevention product blocks an email that contains a file full of national ID numbers. The sender is a regular employee emailing a personal account. What did the control enforce?
choices: The data should not leave by that channel, regardless of the sender's convenience
Personal email is always the approved archive
National ID numbers are public and should be mailed widely
DLP replaces the need to classify data
explanation: DLP watches content and channels. A bulk of ID numbers to a personal account is exfiltration even when the person is an employee. The block is the policy working. Classification is what told DLP the numbers mattered. DLP does not replace classification. It uses it.
choiceNotes: Block the send and follow the incident or exception process. Convenience is not an approved channel.
Personal mail is an uncontrolled copy. It is not the archive.
National ID numbers are sensitive. Mailing them widely is the loss.
DLP needs the classification to know what to block. It does not invent policy by itself.

stem: A team encrypts a database column, masks it in the support tool, and still finds the full values in a debug log that the application writes on error. Where did the protection fail?
choices: Data in use, and in the logs, escaped the controls that covered the column and the support view
The encryption failed because support could not see the numbers
Masking failed because the support tool hid the numbers
Logs are never sensitive
explanation: The column encryption and the mask did their jobs in those two places. The application then wrote the plaintext into a log while handling the data. That is data in use leaking into a store nobody classified. Logs are a common miss. Fix the logging, restrict the log, and treat the existing log as sensitive. Support being unable to see the column is the mask working, not the encryption failing.
choiceNotes: The debug log is the hole. Protect or stop the plaintext logging. The other two controls were never applied to that file.
Support being masked is success of the mask, not failure of the encryption.
Hiding the number in the support tool is what masking is for. The failure is elsewhere.
Logs often contain the very data you tried to keep in one column. They are sensitive when they do.

stem: Which control most directly limits a stolen database file that was already copied off the server, assuming the copy is the ciphertext and the key was not stored beside it?
choices: Encryption of the data at rest, with the key managed elsewhere
A network firewall rule that the thief already bypassed by copying the file
A longer password on the wireless network
A bollard
explanation: Once the file has left, network controls are behind it. Encryption still works if the attacker does not have the key. That is why the key must not sit in the same backup as the ciphertext. A Wi-Fi password and a bollard do not help a file that is already in someone else's hands.
choiceNotes: The ciphertext is unreadable without the key. Key management is part of the control, not an afterthought.
The firewall did not travel with the file. It cannot uncopy the theft.
The wireless password is irrelevant to a file that has already been taken.
A bollard protects a driveway. It does not decrypt or encrypt a database.

stem: Leadership says the business can lose no more than 15 minutes of orders, and the checkout service must be back within one hour. Which metrics are those?
choices: 15 minutes is the recovery point objective. One hour is the recovery time objective
15 minutes is the RTO and one hour is the RPO
Both numbers are the mean time between failures
The RPO is how fast the building's doors must unlock
explanation: RPO is how much data you can lose, measured as time back to the last good copy. RTO is how long you can be down. A nightly backup cannot meet a 15-minute RPO. A cold site cannot meet a one-hour RTO. MTBF is how long a component tends to run between failures. Doors are not the metric.
choiceNotes: Data-loss budget is RPO. Downtime budget is RTO. The sentence maps cleanly onto those two.
Swapping the names swaps the backup design and the failover design. That is a costly mix-up.
MTBF is reliability of a component over a long period. It is not a 15-minute data target.
RPO is about data, not about unlocking a lobby.

stem: A recovery site has racks, power, and cooling, but no hardware and no recent data. The RTO is 30 minutes. Why does the site fail the requirement?
choices: It is a cold site. Thirty minutes is not enough time to buy hardware and restore data
It is a hot site, so it is already serving users
Empty racks are a warm site with a current replica
Cold sites fail over automatically in under a minute
explanation: Cold means space and utilities, not systems. You still procure or ship hardware and restore data. That is days or weeks, not half an hour. A hot site is current and ready. A warm site has equipment and some data, but not a live replica you can cut to in minutes. Automatic one-minute failover is an active design, not a cold room.
choiceNotes: Cold cannot meet a 30-minute RTO. The room is not the system.
A hot site would already have systems and data. Empty racks are not hot.
Warm means hardware is present. Empty racks are colder than that.
Nothing at a cold site fails over by itself. There is nothing running to fail to.

stem: Monday is a full backup. Each later day records only what changed since the day before. The array dies on Friday. What is the minimum set that restores Friday?
choices: Monday's full backup plus every incremental through Friday, in order
Friday's incremental only
Monday only
Any one incremental, because each contains the whole week
explanation: Incrementals are a chain. Friday does not contain Tuesday. Skip a day and the restore has a hole. The full backup alone is a week stale. This is why incremental restores are brittle and why people test them. A differential, by contrast, would need only the full backup and Friday.
choiceNotes: Full plus each later incremental, in order, is the incremental restore.
Friday's incremental contains only Friday's changes, not the rest of the week.
Monday's full backup alone misses the four days of orders that followed it.
An incremental is a delta since the previous backup, not a full copy of the week.

stem: Snapshots of a database volume are taken every hour on the same storage array that holds the volume. An administrator calls the snapshots the backup. The array then fails completely. What is the misconception?
choices: A snapshot on the same array is not an independent backup. The failure took the snapshots with it
Snapshots on the same disks are an offsite copy
An array failure cannot affect snapshots stored on that array
Backups are unnecessary if snapshots exist anywhere on the same shelf
explanation: A snapshot is a fast rollback for mistakes and for some corruption, and it lives with the storage unless you copy it elsewhere. Array loss, site loss, and ransomware that can delete snapshots all defeat a same-box snapshot. A backup is a separate copy, preferably offline or immutable and not in the same failure domain. Test a restore from that other copy.
choiceNotes: The snapshots died with the array. A backup has to be able to survive the thing it is backing up.
Same-array storage is the opposite of offsite.
If the disks are gone, the snapshots on those disks are gone.
A snapshot on the same shelf shares the fate of the shelf. That is not a backup strategy.

stem: Two data centers both serve customers at the same time, and either can carry the full load. What is that availability design?
choices: Active-active
Active-passive
A single cold room
A tape in a drawer
explanation: Active-active means both sites do production work and are sized so one can absorb the other. Active-passive keeps a standby that is not serving. A cold room and a tape are recovery supplies, not a live second site.
choiceNotes: Both sites live, each able to take the full load, is active-active.
Active-passive waits. The standby is not serving customers during normal operation.
A cold room has no running systems, so it is not serving customers at all.
A tape is a backup medium. It is not a second live site.

stem: A team walks through a ransomware scenario in a conference room and writes down who would call the insurer. They do not move any traffic. What did they do, and what did they not prove?
choices: A tabletop exercise. It did not prove the failover commands work
A full failover test, because talking moves production
A penetration test
A cryptographic erase
explanation: A tabletop rehearses decisions without touching production. It finds missing phone numbers and muddy ownership. It does not prove backups restore or that the other site comes up. That takes a failover or a parallel test. A penetration test is an authorized attack simulation. Cryptographic erase destroys data by deleting keys.
choiceNotes: The meeting is a tabletop. Schedule a technical test if you need proof the technology works.
No traffic moved, so this was not a failover. Calling it one leaves you surprised later.
A penetration test tries to find and exploit weaknesses under rules of engagement. A conference room is not that.
Cryptographic erase is a sanitization method. It does not rehearse an incident.

stem: A company runs the same critical application in two cloud providers so that a bug in one provider's platform does not take the service down. What resilience idea is that, beyond simply having two virtual machines in one provider?
choices: Platform diversity
A single availability zone
One shared local administrator password
Disabling backups because two providers exist
explanation: Platform diversity avoids a common-mode failure in one vendor's identity system, network, or hypervisor. Two virtual machines in one zone still share that zone's fate. Diversity costs money and complexity, and it does not replace backups: a bad data change can replicate to both providers. Shared passwords and no backups undo the resilience you just bought.
choiceNotes: Two providers reduce the chance that one platform bug is a total outage. That is diversity, and it is more than two guests on one platform.
One zone is a single failure domain. Diversity means leaving that domain.
A shared password is a common-mode failure of your own making.
Both providers can replicate corrupt data. Backups, ideally immutable, are still required.
